subject: dsp
title: Samples, Signals and Levels
summary: Read sampled data, reason about timing and ambiguity, measure levels and recognise patterns.

lessons.title: Samples on a time axis
lessons.summary: Read a sample record’s timing and distinguish its last timestamp from its duration.
lessons.body:
A **signal** records how a quantity changes. A sensor might measure temperature over time; a synthetic test might contain plain numbers with no physical unit. **Digital signal processing (DSP)** changes or analyses such sequences of values. A **sample** is one value. A **sample index** counts positions, starting at zero here; it is not itself a time in seconds.

A record such as `[2, 4, 1, 3]` contains four samples. Its third value has index 2 because counting starts at zero. The values alone do not say whether the measurements are a second apart or a millisecond apart.

## From count to seconds

For **uniform sampling**, consecutive values are separated by the same **sample period**. The **sample rate** counts samples per second. A higher rate means shorter gaps. This course assumes an exact constant rate unless stated otherwise.

At 4 samples per second, four samples starting at zero have timestamps 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 seconds. Interpreting the same values at twice the rate halves every gap and makes the record pass twice as quickly. Keep the rate, start time and physical units with the data.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Regular snapshots
> Imagine taking a photograph every quarter of a second.
>
> **How it maps:** Each photograph is a sample; its position in the stack is its index. The schedule supplies its time.
>
> **Where it stops:** A sample need not be an image, and equally spaced measurements do not guarantee that fast motion between them can be recovered.

## Duration versus timestamp span

For a non-empty record, this course calls the number of sample periods represented by the record its **record duration**. The last period ends one interval after the final timestamp. The **timestamp span** measures only the gap between the first and last sample. State which one an application needs.

Those four samples represent a one-second record interval, although the last timestamp is 0.75 seconds. Four sample periods fill that interval; the recorded instants have only three gaps. Adding a sample at exactly one second would start the next interval rather than fill a missing slot in the first.

This **half-open interval** includes its start and excludes its end. A one-sample record has one period of duration and zero timestamp span. An empty record has no first or last timestamp.

The reference relationships below collect the timing rules. They assume a non-empty, uniformly sampled record whose first timestamp is zero.

```formula reference
T_s = 1 / F_s
t_n = n / F_s
D = N / F_s
S = (N − 1) / F_s
where
T_s: sample period, in seconds (s)
F_s: sample rate, in samples per second
t_n: timestamp of sample n relative to the first sample, in seconds (s)
n: integer sample index from zero through N − 1
N: positive number of samples in the record
D: record duration, in seconds (s)
S: first-to-last timestamp span, in seconds (s)
s: second, the unit of time
In words: A sample’s position counts the gaps since the start. Record duration counts one period per sample; timestamp span counts one fewer gap. Increasing the sample rate shortens both for the same stored record.
```

Timing metadata does not reveal everything that happened between measurements. Irregular measurements need their actual timestamps rather than one assumed rate.

## Key takeaways
- A sample index is a position; the sample rate converts it to time.
- Record duration counts sample periods, while timestamp span counts gaps.
- Keep timing and physical units alongside a numerical array.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: signal values and sample indices](https://www.dspguide.com/CH2.PDF)

questions.prompt: A logger stores five uniformly spaced samples starting at time zero. Its summary puts the last sample at the end of five sample periods. What is the mistake?

options.text: It should count six periods because indexing starts at zero
options.explanation: Starting at zero does not add a period. The first sample is already present before any gap has elapsed.

options.text: Five timestamps contain only four gaps
options.explanation: Correct. Five periods describe this course’s record duration, while the last timestamp is only four periods after the first.

options.text: The last sample is always one second after the first
options.explanation: The elapsed time depends on sample rate; a sample count alone does not give seconds.

questions.workedExample:
1. Put the first timestamp at zero.
2. Each later sample adds one gap, so five samples provide four gaps.
3. The five-period record interval ends one period after the last timestamp.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: You store the samples for one second at a uniform rate, including the start and excluding the end. A colleague adds another sample at exactly the ending time. What changed?

options.text: They filled a missing slot in the original record
options.explanation: The original half-open interval was complete; its ending timestamp was deliberately excluded.

options.text: They shortened the gaps between all existing samples
options.explanation: Appending a timestamp does not change the spacing or times of the original samples.

options.text: They included the first sample of the next interval
options.explanation: Correct. At the same rate, the extra sample adds another represented sample period beyond the original interval.

questions.workedExample:
1. A half-open interval includes its start and excludes its end.
2. The original record therefore does not need a sample at exactly its ending time.
3. Adding that sample extends the stored record under the same sample-period convention.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: Which statements are valid for a uniformly sampled record? Select all that apply.

options.text: The sample rate must accompany a bare list
options.explanation: Correct. Values alone do not identify their time spacing.

options.text: An empty record has a zero first-to-last span
options.explanation: There is no first or last timestamp in an empty record, so that span is undefined.

options.text: A one-sample record has zero timestamp span
options.explanation: Correct. Its first and last timestamps are the same.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the values from their timing metadata.
2. A non-empty record has a first and last timestamp.
3. With one sample these coincide; with no samples neither exists.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

lessons.title: Sines, cycles and phase
lessons.summary: Describe a sampled sinusoid using amplitude, frequency and phase.
lessons.body:
A **sinusoid** is a smooth repeating wave described by sine or cosine. It is useful as a controlled test signal: its amplitude, frequency and timing can be varied separately. **Amplitude** here means the maximum magnitude of the ideal wave relative to its centre. **Frequency** counts cycles per second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. A 2 Hz wave repeats twice per second.

**Phase** tells us where in the cycle a wave starts. An angle in **radians** measures arc length divided by radius. A full turn is twice pi radians; pi is about 3.14159. A quarter turn is half pi radians. At zero starting phase, sine starts at zero and rises; cosine starts at its positive maximum.

## A wave sampled at regular instants

Imagine sampling one complete cycle at four equally spaced positions. A unit-amplitude sine starting at zero phase gives approximately `[0, 1, 0, -1]`. The next sample begins the next cycle.

Changing amplitude scales the height without changing the repetition rate. Changing frequency changes how far through a cycle each new sample advances. Changing starting phase chooses a different starting point without changing that advance. A quarter-turn starting phase makes this sine start at its positive maximum.

A finite set of samples need not hit the ideal wave’s maximum. Its largest recorded sample can therefore be smaller than the stated amplitude. That alone does not show that the generator used the wrong amplitude.

This reference expression describes the same three controls for a sampled sine:

```formula reference
x[n] = A sin(2πfn / F_s + φ)
0 ≤ n ≤ N − 1
where
x: sampled signal, in the same units as A
n: integer sample index, starting at zero
A: non-negative sinusoid amplitude, in the signal’s units
sin: sine function, taking an angle in radians and returning a unitless value between −1 and 1
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: sinusoid frequency, in hertz (Hz)
F_s: sample rate, in samples per second
φ: starting phase, in radians
N: positive number of samples
Hz: hertz, one cycle per second
In words: Amplitude controls wave height, frequency controls progress through each cycle, and starting phase chooses the initial position. At a fixed sample rate, increasing frequency advances farther through the cycle between samples.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A hand on a clock
> Picture a hand turning at a steady rate.
>
> **How it maps:** Its turning rate represents frequency and its starting direction represents phase. The vertical height of its tip behaves like a sine wave.
>
> **Where it stops:** The rotating hand is a geometric aid; a measured signal does not need to be a physical rotating object.

## Frequency per sample

**Normalised frequency** must name its convention. Here it means cycles per sample; some other texts instead use radians per sample or a fraction of the Nyquist frequency. Never transfer a bare number between these conventions.

One cycle every four sample intervals means one quarter of a cycle per sample. At a fixed frequency in hertz, sampling more often reduces the advance between samples. At a fixed cycles-per-sample frequency, interpreting the same sequence at a higher sample rate makes it repeat faster in physical time.

Always keep the sample rate with a test signal. A waveform’s appearance alone cannot establish its frequency in hertz, and sampling can make different continuous waves look identical, as the next lesson explains.

## Key takeaways
- Amplitude controls height, frequency controls repetition and phase controls the cycle’s starting point.
- Recorded samples can miss the ideal wave’s maximum.
- Always label a normalised-frequency convention.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter](https://www.dspguide.com/CH8.PDF)

questions.prompt: You keep a sine wave’s frequency in hertz fixed and double the sample rate. What happens to its progress through a cycle between neighbouring samples?

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: More frequent samples leave less time for the wave to progress, rather than more.

options.text: It stays the same because the wave frequency is unchanged
options.explanation: The physical frequency is unchanged, but each sample gap is shorter, so cycles per sample changes.

options.text: It halves
options.explanation: Correct. Twice as many sampling intervals fit into the same cycle, so each advances only half as far.

questions.workedExample:
1. Holding hertz fixed keeps each complete cycle the same length in seconds.
2. Doubling sample rate puts twice as many equal gaps within it.
3. Each gap therefore covers half the previous fraction of a cycle.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: A unit-amplitude sine starts at zero phase. You change only its starting phase to a quarter turn. What happens to its first sample?

options.text: It changes from zero to positive one
options.explanation: Correct. Sine of a quarter turn is one.

options.text: It remains zero
options.explanation: Phase controls the starting point, so the initial value can change.

options.text: Its frequency doubles
options.explanation: A constant phase change does not change the angle advance per sample.

questions.workedExample:
1. Zero-phase sine starts at its centre and rises.
2. Advancing its starting position by a quarter turn puts it at the positive maximum.
3. Amplitude and frequency stay unchanged because only starting phase changed.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: A finite sampled sine has an ideal amplitude of 1. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.

options.text: Its largest recorded sample must be exactly 1
options.explanation: Sampling may miss the instant of the ideal maximum.

options.text: Its recorded sample magnitudes cannot exceed 1 in exact arithmetic
options.explanation: Correct. Sine stays between negative one and one.

options.text: For a known nonzero frequency in cycles per sample, changing only the sample rate changes its interpreted hertz value
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed nonzero cycles-per-sample frequency scales with sample rate. This does not claim that a finite sample sequence uniquely identifies its original continuous frequency.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ideal amplitude bounds the exact sine values.
2. A finite sampling grid need not contain a maximum.
3. Physical frequency requires both the sequence and its sample rate.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

lessons.title: When sampling hides frequency
lessons.summary: Recognise aliases and place anti-alias filtering before sampling.
lessons.body:
Uniform samples can agree even when their underlying continuous waves differ. This ambiguity is **aliasing**. Once two possible inputs produce the same samples, analysing those samples alone cannot tell which input occurred. Sampling faster is useful only if it is fast enough for the signal content arriving at the sampler.

## Keep baseband content below half the rate

A **baseband** signal occupies frequencies from zero up to some highest frequency. A **band-limited** ideal signal has no content above that limit. The **Nyquist frequency** is half the sample rate. To preserve arbitrary phase at the upper edge of this baseband signal, its highest frequency must stay strictly below that boundary:

```formula essential
F_s > 2f_max
f_N = F_s / 2
where
F_s: sample rate, in samples per second
f_max: highest frequency present in the ideal baseband signal, in hertz (Hz)
f_N: Nyquist frequency, half the sample rate, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: The sample rate must exceed twice the highest baseband frequency. Keeping the signal below half the sample rate prevents overlap in the ideal band-limited case; the endpoint is excluded here.
```

Why exclude the endpoint? A sine at exactly half the sample rate, with zero starting phase, is sampled at its zero crossings. Every sample is zero in exact arithmetic. A cosine at that same frequency alternates positive and negative values. Merely having two samples per cycle does not preserve every possible phase and amplitude at the boundary.

A finite record is also not the infinite sequence assumed by ideal reconstruction theory. The condition prevents spectral overlap for the ideal band-limited case; it does not promise recovery of arbitrary data from a few samples.

## An explicit fold

At 1000 samples per second, a 700 Hz cosine produces the same samples as a 300 Hz cosine, with equal amplitude and zero starting phase. The higher frequency appears below the 500 Hz Nyquist limit. If both tones arrive together, their stored contributions overlap: a later analysis cannot reliably assign the combined values back to the two original tones.

In this frequency interval the alias behaves like a reflection around half the sample rate. Higher frequencies can fold repeatedly, and phase can change during folding. The example specifies cosine and starting phase to avoid suggesting that every sine keeps its original sign.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A wheel in a film
> A wheel turning quickly can appear to turn slowly or backwards in regularly spaced film frames.
>
> **How it maps:** The frames sample position. Different numbers of turns between frames can produce the same visible positions, just as different frequencies can produce the same samples.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real wheel has visual features and exposure blur. The DSP claim concerns mathematical sample values, not every detail of a video.

## Prevent the ambiguity before it happens

An analogue **anti-alias filter** reduces high-frequency content before an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) takes samples. Real filters need a transition band, so leave room between wanted frequencies and the Nyquist limit. The filter reduces unwanted content to an acceptable level rather than forming an ideal brick-wall cutoff.

A digital filter after this sampling step cannot separate a wanted 300 Hz component from a 700 Hz component already folded onto it. When later reducing a digital sample rate, filtering must likewise precede the rate reduction.

## Key takeaways
- Different continuous frequencies can produce identical samples.
- Use a strict upper frequency margin and account for real anti-alias filter transitions.
- Filtering must act before the sampling operation that would cause the alias.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter](https://www.dspguide.com/CH3.PDF)
- [MIT 6.003: sampling theorem and aliasing](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/12e6e5d7567fca2e993ef8563fef5a60_MIT6_003F11_lec21.pdf)

questions.prompt: At 1000 samples per second, equal-amplitude zero-phase cosines at 700 Hz and 300 Hz produce identical samples. You receive only the stored samples. What can you conclude?

options.text: The original tone must have been 300 Hz
options.explanation: The 700 Hz input is another possible source of exactly the same samples.

options.text: The samples alone cannot choose between those inputs
options.explanation: Correct. Aliasing makes different continuous inputs indistinguishable from their sampled values alone.

options.text: A longer analysis of these same values must reveal 700 Hz
options.explanation: More computation cannot distinguish inputs that produced the same information. Extra knowledge about acquisition would be needed.

questions.workedExample:
1. The question gives two inputs with identical samples.
2. Any analysis using only those samples sees the same values for either input.
3. Acquisition constraints, such as a suitable input filter, can exclude the high-frequency possibility; the bare record cannot.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: A signal may contain an arbitrary-phase sinusoid at exactly 500 Hz. Is sampling at exactly 1000 samples per second sufficient under this lesson’s condition?

options.text: Yes, two samples per cycle always preserve it
options.explanation: At the endpoint a zero-phase sine is sampled only at its zeros.

options.text: Yes, if a digital filter is applied afterwards
options.explanation: Post-sampling filtering cannot restore information already lost.

options.text: No; exceed 1000 and allow a practical filter margin
options.explanation: Correct. The strict condition excludes the endpoint; real filtering needs a transition margin too.

questions.workedExample:
1. Half the proposed rate is exactly 500 Hz.
2. An arbitrary-phase signal includes a zero-phase sine at that frequency.
3. Its samples can all be zero, so the endpoint does not preserve arbitrary amplitude and phase. Choose a higher rate with suitable input filtering.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: A 700 Hz interferer has already folded onto a wanted 300 Hz signal at 1000 samples per second. Which actions address this? Select all that apply.

options.text: On future captures, filter the analogue input before sampling
options.explanation: Correct. Reducing the interferer before sampling prevents this fold from contaminating the wanted band.

options.text: Separate the two original tones perfectly using only a 300 Hz digital notch
options.explanation: A notch removes their combined 300 Hz contribution; it cannot distinguish the originals.

options.text: On future captures, use a sufficiently higher rate with appropriate input filtering
options.explanation: Correct. A changed acquisition design can avoid this particular fold.

questions.workedExample:
1. The stored samples contain a combined contribution at the same apparent frequency.
2. A later filter acts on that combination.
3. Prevention changes what reaches the sampler or changes the sampling design; it cannot retroactively identify the two contributions.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

lessons.title: Quantisation and clipping
lessons.summary: Separate rounding to levels from losing values beyond the range.
lessons.body:
Sampling chooses times. **Quantisation** chooses representable amplitude levels. These are different restrictions: increasing the sample rate does not make the amplitude steps finer. A digital value may represent volts, temperature or a unitless normalised amplitude; know the conversion before interpreting its size.

A **bit** has two possible states. Three bits can label eight different codes. The voltage range, coding and rounding rules still need specification: a bit count alone does not define a complete converter.

## Small rounding errors and lost peaks

Imagine a toy quantiser with levels spaced by 0.25, from −1 to 0.75. An input of 0.30 rounds to 0.25. Small input changes can leave the output unchanged until it crosses the boundary to the next level. Finer steps can preserve smaller amplitude changes within the available range.

An exact halfway input needs a stated tie rule. If this toy chooses the more positive neighbour, −0.375 becomes −0.25 rather than −0.5. Another rule could choose differently. Specify the spacing, endpoints and rounding rule before predicting exact output values; the bit count alone is insufficient.

For nearest-level rounding without range limiting, error magnitude is at most half a step. That bound does not protect over-range inputs. **Clipping**, also called saturation, caps excessive values at an endpoint. In this toy, inputs of 1.0 and 1.5 both become 0.75. Their different peak heights are lost.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Marks and ends on a ruler
> A short ruler has marked divisions and also a final endpoint.
>
> **How it maps:** Rounding a length to the nearest mark resembles quantisation. Reporting every length beyond the ruler as its maximum resembles clipping.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real measurements can have other errors; the ruler comparison does not make quantisation error random or independent.

## Choose the remedy for the problem

If small changes disappear between amplitude levels, consider finer quantisation over the required range. Increasing sample rate alone changes the time spacing, not those levels. Increasing bit depth can provide more levels, but the chosen input range still matters.

If peaks reach the endpoint, reduce input gain before the range-limited stage or choose an appropriate input range. Making an already clipped record quieter only shrinks its flat peaks; it cannot infer their original heights.

Quantisation error also depends on the signal and rounding scheme. A repeated input can produce a repeated error, so do not automatically treat that error as independent white noise. These lessons distinguish the mechanisms rather than assuming a noise model that fits every input.

## Key takeaways
- Sampling selects times; quantisation selects amplitude levels.
- Specify the grid, endpoints and tie rule before predicting a quantiser.
- Clipping can cause errors far larger than half a step and loses information.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter](https://www.dspguide.com/CH3.PDF)

questions.prompt: Two quantisers have the same amplitude levels. They disagree only for inputs exactly halfway between neighbouring levels. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether one takes samples faster
options.explanation: Sample rate describes timing and does not specify how a halfway amplitude is rounded.

options.text: Whether their rounding tie rules differ
options.explanation: Correct. Both neighbouring levels are equally near, so a tie rule determines which is chosen.

options.text: Whether one has removed the signal’s frequency
options.explanation: The disagreement described concerns selection of an amplitude level, not frequency processing.

questions.workedExample:
1. The level grid is the same, so both quantisers have the same neighbours available.
2. Exactly halfway, neither neighbour is nearer.
3. Different tie rules can therefore explain the disagreement without changing sample rate or bit count.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: A range-limited quantiser reports the same maximum output for several different over-range inputs. Why can its error be much larger than half a quantisation step?

options.text: Clipping caps the output even as the input keeps rising
options.explanation: Correct. The small nearest-rounding error bound does not apply to arbitrary inputs beyond the representable range.

options.text: All nearest-level rounding errors must exceed half a step
options.explanation: Within range, nearest-level rounding has at most half a step of error. Clipping is the additional problem here.

options.text: The output silently gains extra levels beyond its maximum
options.explanation: The premise states a range-limited output; it cannot represent those missing levels.

questions.workedExample:
1. Nearest-level rounding chooses a nearby grid value when that value is available.
2. Beyond the range, the output stays at the endpoint instead of following the input.
3. The distance from input to stored output can keep growing, and several peak heights become indistinguishable.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: Which actions or claims are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: Increasing sample rate always reduces amplitude step size
options.explanation: Time spacing and amplitude resolution are different design choices.

options.text: Record the rounding and endpoint rules
options.explanation: Correct. A bit count alone cannot predict exact outputs.

options.text: Lowering gain after clipping cannot restore the lost peak heights
options.explanation: Correct. Several original values already collapsed onto the same endpoint.

questions.workedExample:
1. A sample rate specifies when values are taken.
2. A quantiser specifies which values can be represented.
3. After clipping, original peak heights are ambiguous; multiplying the stored endpoints cannot remove that ambiguity.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

lessons.title: Mean, peak and RMS
lessons.summary: Measure a finite record’s offset and overall level with the correct units.
lessons.body:
One number cannot describe every property of a signal. A sensor record can have a steady offset, a fluctuating component and occasional large excursions. **Record mean**, **peak magnitude** and **root mean square (RMS)** answer different questions. This lesson uses a non-empty finite record of real values; these are exact record descriptions, not estimates of an unknown infinite process.

## Mean and DC offset

The mean adds all samples and divides by the count. **DC** originally means direct current; in DSP a DC component is a constant offset. The record mean is the constant you subtract to centre that record at zero.

For `[1, 3]` volts the mean is 2 volts and the centred samples are `[-1, 1]` volts. The offset might be unwanted sensor bias, or it might be the actual quantity being measured. Do not remove it automatically. A short slice of a changing signal can have a nonzero mean without the underlying source having a permanent offset.

## Peak and RMS

Peak magnitude is the largest absolute sample value. RMS squares the samples, averages the squares and takes a square root. Squaring prevents positive and negative values cancelling. The final root restores the original units.

Mean zero does not mean no signal. A record alternating between −1 and +1 volt has zero mean, but its RMS is 1 volt. The signs cancel in the mean; they do not cancel when squared. Adding a constant offset increases this record’s RMS even though its fluctuations around its own mean stay the same.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A commuter around home
> A commuter travels equal distances east and west of home. Their average signed position can be home even though they spend time far from it.
>
> **How it maps:** Mean uses signed positions, which can cancel. RMS measures distance from zero using squares, so opposite signs cannot erase the excursions. Peak records the farthest position reached.
>
> **Where it stops:** RMS is a particular squared-distance measure, not the average distance travelled or the length of the journey.

These reference expressions show how mean and RMS treat the same record differently:

```formula reference
μ = (Σ x[n]) / N
R = √((Σ x[n]^2) / N)
0 ≤ n ≤ N − 1
where
μ: record mean, in the signal’s units
R: record RMS, in the signal’s units
x: real-valued signal, in physical units or unitless
N: positive number of samples
n: integer sample index from zero through N − 1
Σ: add one term for each integer n in the stated range
√: non-negative square root
In words: Mean describes a record’s signed offset. RMS combines its offset and fluctuations without cancelling opposite signs, then returns the result in the original signal units.
```

## Choose the measurement for the decision

Use mean to examine offset, peak to check stored excursions against a limit, and RMS to describe overall squared level. Records with the same RMS can have different peaks, so an RMS limit alone does not guarantee freedom from clipping. Use the same measurement window when comparing records.

RMS has a connection to physical power only with a specified model, such as voltage across a fixed resistor. Squared temperature values are not automatically watts. Peak sample magnitude also need not equal the maximum of a continuous waveform between sampling instants.

## Key takeaways
- Mean describes offset; subtracting it changes the measured signal.
- Peak checks extremes; RMS includes both offset and fluctuations.
- Mean, peak and RMS retain the original signal units.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter](https://www.dspguide.com/CH2.PDF)

questions.prompt: A voltage record alternates equally between positive and negative values of the same nonzero size. Its mean meter reads zero. Which interpretation is sound?

options.text: Every sample must be zero
options.explanation: Positive and negative values can cancel in the mean even while the signal continues to fluctuate.

options.text: Its RMS must also be zero because signs cancel
options.explanation: RMS squares values first, so negative values do not cancel positive ones.

options.text: Its RMS can reveal a nonzero level despite zero mean
options.explanation: Correct. Mean describes signed offset; RMS retains the nonzero contribution of both signs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Equal positive and negative values cancel when averaged with their signs.
2. Squaring makes both contributions positive.
3. The RMS is therefore nonzero and remains measured in volts after the square root.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: A sensor record contains fluctuations plus a nonzero constant offset. You subtract this record’s mean. Which statement describes its centred RMS?

options.text: It measures the remaining fluctuations around the removed mean
options.explanation: Correct. Subtracting the mean centres the record and removes its offset contribution from RMS.

options.text: It must be zero because the centred mean is zero
options.explanation: Zero mean does not remove fluctuations or make their squared values cancel.

options.text: It still includes the same constant offset contribution
options.explanation: The constant offset represented by the record mean was subtracted from every sample.

questions.workedExample:
1. The original RMS includes both offset and fluctuations.
2. Subtracting the record mean removes that record’s constant offset.
3. The remaining RMS describes the centred fluctuations. Whether removing that offset is useful depends on what the sensor is meant to measure.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

questions.prompt: Which conclusions are safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: A zero mean proves every sample is zero
options.explanation: Positive and negative samples can cancel in the mean.

options.text: RMS of a voltage record is measured in volts
options.explanation: Correct. The square root restores the input unit.

options.text: A short record’s mean need not equal a permanent sensor bias
options.explanation: Correct. Record boundaries and changing signals affect the average.

questions.workedExample:
1. Check what each statistic actually computes.
2. Mean can cancel signs; RMS cannot cancel their squares.
3. RMS retains voltage units, while interpreting a measured mean as permanent bias requires knowledge beyond that short record.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

lessons.title: Decibels need a reference
lessons.summary: Interpret level changes by naming the measured quantity and its reference.
lessons.body:
A **decibel (dB)** expresses a ratio on a logarithmic scale. It makes large ratios manageable and turns successive multiplicative gains into additive level changes. A bare decibel value is incomplete unless you know what is compared: power, amplitude, or a level relative to a named reference.

Zero decibels means equal numerator and reference, not silence. Negative decibels mean the numerator is smaller than its reference. They do not mean a negative amplitude or negative physical power.

## Power and amplitude are different

For positive powers, a tenfold increase is +10 dB and a tenfold decrease is −10 dB. For amplitude magnitudes such as voltage, a tenfold increase is +20 dB. Do not apply an amplitude rule to a power ratio.

The different scales agree when power is proportional to amplitude squared with the same proportionality factor. For example, halving an RMS voltage across the same resistance quarters the power; both describe about a 6 dB decrease. Across different resistances, the voltage ratio alone does not establish the power ratio.

The reference expressions use a **logarithm**, which asks which power of ten produces a ratio. They are useful for converting a measured ratio, rather than memorising separate answers for every possible change.

```formula reference
L_P = 10 log_10(P / P_ref)
where
L_P: power level relative to the reference, in decibels (dB)
P: positive measured power, in the same units as P_ref
P_ref: positive reference power
log_10: base-ten logarithm of a positive unitless ratio
dB: decibel, one tenth of a bel, the logarithmic ratio unit
In words: A tenfold power increase raises the level by ten decibels. Equal power and reference give zero decibels; a smaller positive power gives a negative level.
```

For positive amplitude magnitudes of the same kind, the conventional amplitude-ratio expression uses twenty:

```formula reference
L_A = 20 log_10(A / A_ref)
where
L_A: amplitude level relative to the reference, in decibels (dB)
A: positive measured amplitude magnitude, such as RMS voltage
A_ref: positive reference amplitude of the same kind and unit as A
log_10: base-ten logarithm of a positive unitless ratio
dB: decibel, the logarithmic ratio unit
In words: A tenfold amplitude increase raises the level by twenty decibels. Halving amplitude lowers it by about six decibels; this agrees with the power change when power follows amplitude squared with the same proportionality factor.
```

Successive gains add as decibel changes: a 6 dB increase followed by a 6 dB decrease returns to the original level if the stages apply those gains without clipping or other changes. That does not mean adding the decibel readings of two separate signals predicts their mixed level; their timing and phase also matter.

Do not compare peak amplitude to an RMS reference without saying so. A reference of 1 volt RMS produces a different statement from a reference of 1 unitless peak amplitude, even if both ratios happen to have the same number.

## Zero and digital full scale

The logarithm of zero has no finite real value. As a positive amplitude approaches zero, its decibel level decreases without a finite lower limit. For a display, report silence separately or choose and label a display floor. A floor is a display policy, not a measured nonzero signal.

**dBFS** means decibels relative to digital full scale. Metering conventions differ, especially for RMS sine references. In this course’s simple unitless peak meter, full-scale peak magnitude is 1 and the amplitude reference is that same value. A peak of 0.5 is about −6 dB relative to full-scale peak. This definition does not assert a universal sine-RMS convention.

Write the ratio and reference in measurement reports so another person can reproduce the level.

## Key takeaways
- Use ten for power ratios and twenty for amplitude ratios under the stated interpretation.
- Name the reference and whether amplitude means peak or RMS.
- Zero needs deliberate handling; a display floor is a policy.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: power and amplitude decibels](https://www.dspguide.com/CH14.PDF)
- [Analog Devices AN-938: full-scale and RMS conventions](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/app-notes/an-938.pdf)

options.text: Halving voltage quarters power; the two ratios need different dB rules

options.text: A smaller voltage must produce a positive level change
options.explanation: A smaller positive numerator than reference gives a negative level change, whether the ratio concerns amplitude or power.

2. Across the same resistance, its halving quarters power.
3. Apply the amplitude rule to voltage or the power rule to power; both describe about a 6 dB decrease when used with the matching ratio.

lessons.title: Gain, mixing and delay
lessons.summary: Change values and timing while stating what happens at record edges.
lessons.body:
Many DSP tasks begin with simple operations: scale one record, add two records, or shift a record in time. Specify units and timing before combining arrays. Adding a temperature in degrees to an acceleration in metres per second squared has no physical meaning without an explicit model or conversion.

## Scale and mix aligned records

**Gain** multiplies every sample by a factor. A negative gain reverses polarity, swapping positive and negative values. **Mixing** here means adding aligned samples, possibly with separate gains. It does not mean interleaving two arrays or appending one after another.

For the unitless records `[1, -1]` and `[1, 1]`, adding corresponding values gives `[2, 0]`. Equal positive samples reinforce; opposite samples cancel. Two records each within a normalised limit of 1 can therefore sum beyond that limit. Scaling before a range-limited output provides **headroom**, a margin below the allowed peak.

For example, reducing both inputs before mixing can leave room for aligned peaks. Reducing gain after a range-limited stage has already clipped does not restore the original sum. The point at which gain is applied matters.

Equal array lengths alone do not establish that timestamps agree. Two sensors can store the same number of values at different rates or with different starting times. Align what each position represents before adding it. Appending one record after another is concatenation, a different operation from mixing.

## Delay with explicit boundaries

A **sample delay** makes an event occur later. For an integer delay, retrieve an earlier input value at each output index. This lesson treats values outside the finite input record as zero, called **zero extension**.

For input `[1, 2, 3]` and a two-sample delay, retaining only three output samples gives `[0, 0, 1]`. Retaining the complete delayed finite record gives `[0, 0, 1, 2, 3]`. This is a storage choice: the last two original values were cropped in the short output, not destroyed by the delay itself.

A delay measured in samples needs a sample rate to become a time. At a higher rate, the same number of delayed samples represents a shorter wait. A pure delay changes when events occur without changing their order or playing them more slowly.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A recording with a later start
> Imagine placing a recorded announcement two seconds later on a timeline.
>
> **How it maps:** A delay changes the announcement’s position. Saving only the original time window can crop the end, while extending the timeline retains it.
>
> **Where it stops:** This models a pure shift, not echoes, speed changes or the physical propagation of sound.

Shifting values from the end back to the start would be a **circular shift**, a different boundary convention. It can create a value at the beginning where a delayed recording should still be silent. Fractional-sample delay requires estimating values between sample positions and is outside this lesson.

## Key takeaways
- Mixing adds aligned compatible samples; gains control their contributions.
- Sample addition can exceed individual input peaks.
- State the delay’s boundary convention and whether the output retains its tail.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter](https://www.dspguide.com/CH5.PDF)

questions.prompt: Two aligned records each stay within an output stage’s allowed peak. Their positive peaks occur together and you mix them by adding corresponding samples. What should you expect?

options.text: Mixing appends the second record after the first
options.explanation: Appending is concatenation; mixing adds aligned samples at the same times.

options.text: The individual peak limits guarantee the sum will fit
options.explanation: Aligned positive values reinforce, so fitting each input separately does not establish that their sum fits.

options.text: The sum can exceed the limit, so plan headroom before output
options.explanation: Correct. Gain before the range-limited output can leave room for reinforcing peaks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Mixing adds values that represent the same time.
2. Two positive peaks therefore reinforce.
3. Check the possible sum and choose gain before the output stage clips; a later gain reduction cannot recover clipped peak heights.

options.explanation: Correct. The first output uses an out-of-record input and is zero; the original final value lies beyond the retained window.
This wraps the final value to the start instead of using zero extension.

lessons.title: Complex numbers as two components
lessons.summary: Read real and imaginary parts, magnitude, conjugation and a rotating phasor.
lessons.body:
A **complex number** stores two real components in one mathematical object. The **real part** lies on a horizontal axis and the **imaginary part** lies on a perpendicular vertical axis. Imaginary does not mean erroneous or physically impossible: it names a second mathematical direction. DSP uses these pairs to retain the strength and phase of sinusoidal components.

## Two coordinates, one number

The imaginary unit is the number whose square is negative one. Engineers often write it as j. Think of the components as coordinates, rather than two ordinary magnitudes to add. The **complex magnitude** is the straight-line distance from the origin. Its units are the same as the components’ units.

For a real part of 3 and an imaginary part of 4, the magnitude is 5, not 7. Adding complex values instead adds the two real parts and the two imaginary parts separately.

The **complex conjugate** keeps the real part and reverses the imaginary part’s sign. Our example becomes real part 3 and imaginary part −4. It reflects across the real axis while keeping the same magnitude. These reference expressions collect the coordinate rules:

```formula reference
j^2 = −1
z = a + jb
|z| = √(a^2 + b^2)
z_bar = a − jb
where
j: imaginary unit, whose square is −1
z: complex number; its two components share the same units, or are both unitless
a: real component of z
b: imaginary component of z
|z|: non-negative magnitude of z, in the same units as its components
√: non-negative square root
z_bar: complex conjugate of z, formed by reversing the imaginary component’s sign
In words: Real and imaginary components are perpendicular coordinates. Magnitude is the distance from the origin, rather than their sum. Conjugation flips the imaginary direction while preserving that distance.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Directions on a map
> A location three blocks east and four blocks north has two coordinates. Its straight-line distance from the starting point is five blocks.
>
> **How it maps:** The two map directions represent real and imaginary components. Reflecting north to south resembles complex conjugation.
>
> **Where it stops:** Complex multiplication has specific rotation and scaling rules; map coordinates alone do not explain all complex arithmetic.

## A rotating phasor

A **phasor** represents a magnitude and a phase angle together. Picture an arrow from the origin to a complex point. Its length is magnitude and its direction is phase. When an arrow of fixed length rotates, its horizontal and vertical components change even though its magnitude does not. One component alone therefore cannot describe the complete arrow.

At one cycle per four samples, starting along the positive real axis, the phasor visits right, up, left and down. Its real part follows cosine, its imaginary part follows sine. Reversing the imaginary sign reverses the direction of rotation. Later Fourier lessons use complex weights to compare data against such rotations; no transform knowledge is needed yet.

The zero complex number has magnitude zero but no unique direction. An angle returned for zero by software should not be treated as evidence of a meaningful physical phase.

## Key takeaways
- A complex number has real and imaginary components.
- Magnitude combines perpendicular components; conjugation flips the imaginary sign.
- A rotating phasor packages cosine and sine while retaining phase information.

## Further reading
- [Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter](https://www.dspguide.com/CH30.PDF)

questions.prompt: A complex reading has nonzero real and imaginary components. A display adds their absolute values and calls the result its magnitude. What is wrong?

options.text: Magnitude should use only the real component
options.explanation: Both components contribute to the distance from the origin; discarding the imaginary component loses part of the reading.

options.text: Perpendicular components must combine as a straight-line distance
options.explanation: Correct. Adding their absolute values measures travel along the axes, rather than the complex point’s distance from the origin.

options.text: Magnitude must become negative when either component is negative
options.explanation: Magnitude is a non-negative distance, even when one or both coordinates are negative.

questions.workedExample:
1. Real and imaginary parts point along perpendicular axes.
2. Magnitude is the direct distance from the origin to their combined point.
3. Adding the two absolute component values instead follows an indirect route along the axes, so it is the wrong measurement.

options.text: Real −2; imaginary +3

options.text: Real 2; imaginary +3

lessons.title: Find a template with correlation
lessons.summary: Interpret a sliding template match without mistaking a large score for proof.
lessons.body:
**Cross-correlation** scores how well a known **template** matches data at different shifts. A distinctive sensor pulse may be recognisable even when its starting position is unknown. At each shift, multiply aligned values and add them. A strong positive score can indicate a positive match, but raw score also depends on amplitude, offset and overlap length.

## Define the lag before interpreting it

This lesson uses real, unitless finite sequences and the sign convention of SciPy’s `correlate(data, template)`. Treat values outside either stored record as zero. **Lag** is the integer shift of the template relative to the data origin; a positive lag places the template’s start later in the data.

For data `[0, 0, 1, -1, 0]` and template `[1, -1]`, the complete pattern starts at data index 2. The best positive match is therefore at lag +2 samples. At that position, positive aligns with positive and negative with negative; both products contribute positively. Shifting the template one place either way aligns opposite signs and gives a negative score.

For complex inputs, SciPy conjugates the shifted template before multiplying. Conjugation reverses the imaginary sign; it leaves a real template unchanged, so the real-valued example needs no extra operation. Reversing the input order reverses the lag interpretation. Never guess the sign from the word correlation alone.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Sliding a transparent pattern
> Slide a transparent strip with a distinctive pattern across a longer strip and look for alignment.
>
> **How it maps:** The short strip is the template; its position is lag. Correlation combines agreement over corresponding positions into one score.
>
> **Where it stops:** Numerical products allow negative values, amplitude weighting and cancellation. A visual match alone does not define those arithmetic rules.

Do not assume that the position in a returned score array is the lag. Full correlation includes partial overlaps before the template reaches the data’s start, so its lag labels can begin below zero. Obtain the labels explicitly; SciPy provides `correlation_lags` for this purpose.

## Similarity is not a guarantee

Doubling the data amplitude doubles every raw score, including negative scores. An increased peak therefore does not necessarily mean a closer match in shape. A large DC offset can dominate scores when the template has a nonzero mean. Subtracting appropriate means can help compare fluctuating shape, but also changes what is being detected.

Normalising by the overlapping magnitudes can reduce amplitude dependence. The method must specify which overlap is measured and what happens when it contains only zeros, where division by its magnitude would fail. No such normalisation is applied here.

At extreme full-mode lags only a few samples overlap. Their scores are not automatically comparable to a full-template overlap. `valid` mode excludes positions requiring zero padding, provided the data is at least as long as the template. Repeated patterns or noise can produce misleading peaks; report ambiguity rather than assuming a single physical delay.

Correlation compares a sliding template in its original order. **Convolution**, introduced next module, uses a reversal in the sliding sum and describes how a system combines shifted responses. They share arithmetic ingredients but have different index definitions and purposes.

## Key takeaways
- State input order, lag convention and record boundaries.
- Obtain lag labels explicitly rather than using an output array index.
- Raw correlation depends on shape, amplitude, offset and overlap; a peak is evidence to interpret.

## Further reading
- [SciPy: correlation definition and boundary modes](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.correlate.html)
- [SciPy: explicit correlation lag labels](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.correlation_lags.html)

questions.prompt: Using correlate(data, template) with this lesson’s convention, data is `[0, 0, 1, -1, 0]` and template is `[1, -1]`. At which lag does the complete matching template start?

options.text: −2 samples
options.explanation: That reverses the stated convention: this template is later in the data.

options.text: +2 samples
options.explanation: Correct. Template index zero aligns with data index two.

options.text: +3 samples
options.explanation: This aligns the first template value with the negative data value instead.

questions.workedExample:
1. Find the start of the matching pair in the data: index two.
2. The template must move two sample positions later to align there.
3. Under the stated input order and convention, that is positive lag two, rather than necessarily output-array position two.

options.text: It becomes four times as large
options.explanation: Only one of the two factors in each product was doubled.

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: Correct. Each product contains one data value, so every product and its sum doubles.

questions.prompt: Which issues can make a large raw correlation peak misleading? Select all that apply.

options.text: A DC offset with a nonzero-mean template
options.explanation: Correct. Constant contributions can raise raw scores without matching the fluctuating shape.

options.text: Different overlap lengths near full-mode edges
options.explanation: Correct. Extreme lags compare fewer pairs and require careful interpretation.

options.text: Having explicit lag labels
options.explanation: Lag labels prevent a sign/index mistake; they do not create a misleading match.
